You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
The failing test expects an IllegalArgumentException to be thrown when the initial interval is invalid (min > max) or when the function values at the interval endpoints or the initial guess do not bracket a root (i.e., they have the same sign).

According to the current bug report, the Javadoc for the solve method with signature 
`solve(UnivariateRealFunction f, double min, double max, double initial)` 
states that if the function values at the three points (min, max, initial) all have the same sign, it should throw an IllegalArgumentException. However, this condition is not even checked in the implementation.

Inspecting the implementation of this solve method reveals the following relevant behavior:

- It calls `verifySequence(min, initial, max);` (line 103) to verify the order of the parameters. This should catch the case where min > max or initial not in correct order.

- It then checks if the initial guess or endpoints are close enough to a root (line 106-129) and returns the root if so.

- The code checks if the initial and min endpoints bracket a root by checking if their function values have opposite signs (line 120). If so, it delegates to another solve method with bracketing information.

- The code similarly checks if the initial and max endpoints bracket a root (line 132).

- However, if neither the pair (min, initial) nor (initial, max) bracket a root (i.e., function values do not have opposite signs), the code proceeds to call the full Brent algorithm solve (line 138) without throwing an exception.

Therefore, the failing test's scenario where no bracket exists among the three points does not produce an IllegalArgumentException as stated in the documentation, explaining the test failure.

In summary, the root cause is that the solve method does not explicitly check that the function values at min, max, and initial points bracket a root and throw IllegalArgumentException otherwise, despite the method documentation promising this behavior.

Recent bug reports do not appear relevant to this particular issue. The failed test and the current bug report, together with the source snippet, make the root cause clear.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test expects the BrentSolver.solve(UnivariateRealFunction, double, double, double) method to throw an IllegalArgumentException when the initial guess and interval endpoints do not bracket a root (i.e., their function values have the same sign). The bug report complains that the Javadoc claims such an exception is thrown, but this case is not checked in the code. Inspection of the solve method shows that it verifies the order of min, initial, and max but does not verify that function values at these points bracket a root. It checks only partial bracketing cases (min & initial or initial & max) but does not throw an exception if no such bracket exists among the three points. Instead, it calls the full Brent algorithm, violating the contract and causing the test to fail. Hence, the missing validation of bracketing conditions before proceeding to root finding explains the failure.

Suggest fix locations?

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
